title: Altitude sickness: how to recognize it (AMS, HACE, HAPE)
asks: headache and nausea at high elevation
how do I know if I have altitude sickness
short of breath at rest in the mountains
friend is stumbling and confused at 12000 feet
coughing and cant catch breath at high camp
answer: Acute mountain sickness (AMS): at altitude (2,500 meters, about 8,200 feet, or higher), a headache plus at least one of these: weakness or lightheadedness, nausea or vomiting, loss of appetite, fatigue. AMS generally does not occur below 2,000 meters.
AMS typically starts within 1 to 6 hours of reaching altitude, but can be delayed up to 48 hours.

High altitude cerebral edema (HACE, swelling of the brain): usually AMS that gets worse, with headache, altered mental status and loss of coordination (ataxia). Confusion, loss of coordination or changes in consciousness require urgent medical attention.

High altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE, fluid in the lungs): shortness of breath at rest, cough, decreased exercise tolerance or weakness, chest tightness or congestion. The earliest symptoms are commonly decreased exercise tolerance and shortness of breath at rest. Signs include crackles or wheezing in the chest, blue lips or fingertips, and fast heartbeat and breathing.
HAPE often appears on the second night at a higher sleeping altitude, and in 50% of cases it appears without AMS or HACE.
Dehydration can mimic AMS and HACE. Other things that look similar include head trauma, migraine, alcohol hangover, carbon monoxide poisoning, viral illness, hyperthermia and hypothermia.
warnings: HACE and HAPE are life-threatening medical emergencies, and both require evacuation. Untreated, HAPE can be rapidly fatal (6-12 hours).
Untreated AMS increases the risk of HACE. In a few people AMS progresses to HACE or HAPE.
Normally, the most appropriate treatment in all altitude illnesses is to descend.

quotes.text: Acute Mountain Sickness Diagnosis Criteria at altitude (2500M or higher) Headache plus at least one of these: Weakness/lightheadedness Nausea/vomiting Anorexia Fatigue

AMS typically presents within 1-6 hours of altitude exposure although delayed presentations can occur at up to 48 hours. This is a clinical diagnosis of a syndrome consisting of headache, in addition to one or more additional symptoms including: lassitude/ fatigue/ weakness, nausea/ vomiting, anorexia, fatigue, and dizziness/ lightheadedness.

AMS generally does not occur below an altitude of 2000m. When diagnosing AMS, consider ruling out other differentials with similar presentations: dehydration, head trauma, caffeine withdrawal, migraine, alcohol hangover (veisalgia), carbon monoxide poisoning, viral syndrome, emotional stress, hyperthermia, and hypothermia.
Signs and symptoms of dehydration can mimic those of AMS and HACE; however, dehydration itself has not been shown to increase the incidence of AMS.

HACE generally presents as a progression from AMS, although isolated HACE presentations have been reported. HACE is a clinical diagnosis and classically presents with headache, altered mental status and ataxia.

High-Altitude Cerebral Edema is a severe and life-threatening condition that can occur at high elevations, typically above 3,000 meters (9,800 feet). It involves swelling of the brain and can lead to neurological symptoms.

Monitor Neurological Symptoms. Keep a close watch on the person's neurological symptoms. Signs of severe neurological impairment, such as confusion, loss of coordination, or changes in consciousness, require urgent medical attention.

HAPE is life threatening and early diagnosis is critical. The international diagnostic criteria for HAPE are a combination of two signs and two symptoms. The symptoms are dyspnea at rest, cough, decreased exercise tolerance or weakness, and chest tightness or congestion. The earliest symptoms are commonly decreased exercise tolerance and dyspnea at rest. Signs include crackles or wheezing in at least one field. Central cyanosis, tachycardia, and tachypnea.
High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema is a serious condition that can occur at higher elevations, typically above 2,500 meters (8,200 feet).

Monitor Breathing. Keep a close watch on the person's breathing. If there are signs of severe respiratory distress, such as blue lips or fingertips, it may indicate a critical situation, and professional medical help should be sought immediately.
HAPE presents in isolation from AMS/HACE in 50% of cases and will often present on the second night of higher sleeping altitude exposure.
HAPE is a medical emergency, and prompt action is crucial. While these first aid measures can provide initial assistance, professional medical help should be sought without delay.
HACE is a critical condition, and time is of the essence. While these first aid measures can provide initial assistance, medical assistance should be sought urgently.
In a few Soldiers, AMS can progress to life threatening HACE or HAPE, both of which require evacuation.
Untreated, HAPE can be rapidly fatal (6-12 hours) and is the most common cause of death among the altitude illness syndromes.
While at altitude, continue to reassess for AMS, considering differentials that may mimic AMS. Untreated AMS increases risk of HACE, whether AMS is diagnosed or not.

Serious complications of high-altitude disease can be avoided by appropriate preparation, early surveillance of symptom onset, and aggressive treatment of disease. Normally, the most appropriate treatment in all altitude illnesses is to descend.

EARLY SIGNS OF HAPE: JTS says decreased exercise tolerance and shortness of breath at rest; ATP 3-50.21 (2018) lists loss of appetite, low energy level, coughing spasms and a headache. HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 and FEMA P-2064 (2020) have nothing on altitude illness.
